region.note: Region labels are generated automatically: the molecules on the map are split into {k} small clusters; if, in a cluster, more than half of the molecules have a predicted probability of at least 50% for a descriptor and this share is at least 1.5 times that of the whole library, the cluster is named after the qualifying descriptor with the highest share; neighboring clusters with the same name are merged. With the same rule the odor map gets {o} region labels and the structure map only {s}.
params.title: Map settings
params.text: Both maps are UMAP projections to two dimensions with a fixed random seed. Three settings of UMAP's two key parameters (number of neighbors, minimum distance) were tried: (15, 0.1), (30, 0.3) and (50, 0.5). The choice used the validation set only, by the share with at least one common label: each map takes its own best setting, so that the structure map, the control, also performs at its best. The parameters were chosen before the non-flavor molecules were removed; the table shows the validation results recomputed after the removal. The metrics are explained in 5.3.
params.valid: Validation (at least one common label / mean Jaccard)
results.title: Odor overlap of map neighbors
results.intro: The test: for each of the {n} molecules in the odor predictor's scaffold-split test set, take the {k} nearest molecules with true odor labels on the 2-D map, and compute the share of them that have at least one true label in common with it, and the mean Jaccard overlap of the labels. True labels are only used for this calculation and are not shown on the page. The test set was computed once, after both maps' parameters were fixed.
results.take: The odor map beats the structure map on both metrics, and neither 95% confidence interval of the difference (paired bootstrap, 5,000 resamples) includes 0; both maps are far above random picks ({rnd}). Projecting to two dimensions loses some neighborhood information, more so for structure: from {sh} to {sm} for structure, only from {oh} to {om} for odor.
supp.summary: Supplementary metric: agreement of the main predicted descriptor (partly circular)
supp.text: For all {n} molecules, the share of the {k} nearest neighbors on the map whose main predicted descriptor (the one with the highest predicted probability) is the same: odor map {o}, structure map {s}. This metric favors the odor map by construction, because the odor map is drawn from these very predictions, so it is only a supplement and not evidence for the conclusion.
limits.1: The map shows the odor representation learned by a model, not a measurement of human odor perception.
limits.2: UMAP distorts distances: local neighborhoods are fairly reliable, but long distances and the relative positions of regions should not be interpreted.
limits.3: Odor predictions have errors, and the positions and colors inherit them; errors may be larger for molecules not used in training.
limits.4: The map covers organic molecules only. Small inorganic odorants such as hydrogen sulfide are not included, although they matter in some foods: hydrogen sulfide, for example, is linked to the cooked and sulfurous notes of heated and UHT milk.
limits.5: Colors and positions reflect odor categories only, not odor intensity, thresholds or the actual contribution in a food.
excluded.note: This map uses the same library as the flavor ingredient finder: {total} organic molecules. {n} non-flavor molecules were removed: inorganic substances without carbon (including inorganic odorants such as hydrogen sulfide, ammonia and sulfur dioxide), organosilicon compounds (e.g. D6 siloxane, a common GC-MS column-bleed impurity), non-volatile substances, and entries that appear in the original data only as mixtures (their odor labels describe the mixture, not a single molecule).

footer.data: Data and acknowledgements: odor predictions come from the graph neural network of this site's odor predictor, trained on data from The Good Scents Company and Leffingwell & Associates (Sanchez-Lengeling et al., 2019, arXiv:1910.10685, CC BY-NC), curated and merged by OpenPOM (Barsainyan et al., 2023); the raw odor labels are not redistributed here and the page shows model predictions only. The model and its predictions are for non-commercial academic demonstration only.
footer.ref: Related work: Lee BK, Mayhew EJ, Sanchez-Lengeling B, et al. A principal odor map unifies diverse tasks in olfactory perception. Science 2023, 381(6661): 999-1006. doi:10.1126/science.ade4401. This page borrows the idea, drawn with this site's model predictions and UMAP; it does not show results of that paper.

footer.short: Positions and colors are predictions, not measurements. Odor model CC BY-NC, non-commercial academic demo only. See method & sources.
about.practice: Molecules that differ in structure but smell alike are mainly useful as substitutes: when the original is restricted by regulation, a substitute may be allowed, or may cost less or be more stable. They also help in understanding how odor relates to structure, which gives ideas for flavor optimization and fragrance design.
